title: Foundations: Country Ballads - The Complete Guide
summary: What Country Ballads is, where it came from, and how its songs work.
body:
Country Ballads songs: Country ballads are three chords and the truth, sung slow: steel guitar crying, a story of love or loss, and a voice that means every word. Patsy Cline and George Jones set the bar.

History: The Nashville Sound (late 1950s) smoothed country's edges with strings and background vocals; the outlaw movement (1970s) roughed them back up. Ballads remained country's heart throughout.

How the songs work: Country Ballads favors the keys of G, D, C, A, E. Common forms include Verse-chorus with a steel-guitar intro; Story verses, crying chorus. Players should master pedal steel: bending into notes like a voice first, then the nashville number system for session charts. Capo 2 for sweet open-string ballads.

summary: An original Country Ballads study in D drilling the nashville number system for session charts.
body:

title: Crazy - Country Ballads Song Study
summary: Harmonic blueprint and playing guide for Crazy by Patsy Cline (Willie Nelson) (1961).
body:
Crazy — Patsy Cline (Willie Nelson), 1961. Willie wrote it; Patsy's version is immortal.

HARMONIC BLUEPRINT (study chart, key of C):
C | F | G | C

This study chart uses the 'Classic I–IV–V' progression, the Country Ballads workhorse, to map how songs like this move. Form: verse-chorus with a steel-guitar intro. Listen for harmony vocals a third above — it is the fingerprint of the style.

TO PLAY IT: set your tempo to the Country Ballads pocket, voice the chords cleanly, and let harmony vocals a third above. Capo 2 for sweet open-string ballads. (Song facts: title/artist/year are documented public records; the chart is an original study arrangement.)
